1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. AI: artificial intelligence; RACI: responsible, accountable, consulted, informed; SOP: standard operating procedure; KPI: key performance indicator

  • How to use Claude to analyze requirements and clarify a request before work starts
  • How to identify good use cases for Claude and screen out poor ones
  • How to use Claude for research and planning
  • How to improve a process step by step and measure the result

2Analyzing Requirements

Running case

Cedarbrook's Returns Overhaul

  • Customer care says: "Returns take too long and customers complain."
  • The project manager asks Claude to turn the complaint into requirements: who is affected, what "too long" means, what must not change, and what success looks like
  • The result is a short requirements list and eight open questions to take to stakeholders

Claude can help you move from a vague wish to a clear, testable requirement.

Use Claude to Example prompt
Clarify the goal "Restate this request in one sentence and list what is unclear"
List stakeholders and needs "Who is affected by a returns change? What does each need?"
Turn notes into requirements "From these interview notes, list functional needs, constraints and assumptions"
Write user stories and acceptance criteria "Write stories in the form 'As a ..., I want ..., so that ...' with pass/fail criteria"
Find gaps and conflicts "Which requirements conflict or are ambiguous?"
Prepare questions "List the questions I should ask the warehouse manager"
Spot risks "What could go wrong, and what would we see first?"
  • Ask Claude to separate facts you gave from assumptions it made. Review and correct the assumptions.
  • Requirements belong to the stakeholders, not to Claude. Claude drafts and challenges; people confirm.
  • Measure success with numbers: "reduce average return processing from 9 days to 4".
Exam tip

Analyzing requirements with Claude means clarifying, structuring and surfacing gaps, then validating with people. It does not mean Claude decides what the business needs.

3Identifying Good Use Cases

Not every task suits Claude. Screen candidates on value, fit and risk.

Strong fit for Claude Weak fit or needs care
Text-heavy work: drafting, summarizing, classifying, rewriting Tasks needing exact, auditable calculation without verification
Repetitive tasks with a clear pattern Decisions with legal, medical or financial consequences made by Claude alone
Tasks where a person reviews the result Sensitive data that policy does not allow in the tool (Module 13)
Work that is slow because of reading and writing Tasks needing real-time systems or actions Claude is not connected to
Brainstorming and planning support Tasks where an error would be unnoticed and costly
  • Ask: How much time does it take now? How often? What is the cost of a mistake? Who reviews? Is the data allowed?
  • Start with low-risk, high-value use cases, learn from them and expand.
  • Keep a human in the loop wherever errors matter.
  • Not every problem is an AI problem: sometimes a simpler fix (a template, a checklist) works better.

4Research and Planning

Research. Choose the tool by the question (Module 6): web search for a quick fact, Research for a comprehensive cited report. For good results:

  • State the question, scope, time frame and audience
  • Ask for sources and disagreements between sources
  • Separate findings from recommendations
  • Verify the key claims in the cited sources (Module 4)

Planning. Claude is a strong drafting partner for plans.

Plan element Ask Claude for You check
Scope and goals Objectives, in-scope and out-of-scope Matches the sponsor's intent
Work breakdown Phases, tasks, dependencies Nothing missing; realistic order
Timeline Milestones with durations Durations against real capacity
Roles A RACI chart Real people and authority
Risks Risks, likelihood, impact, mitigation Missed risks specific to your context
Communication Update cadence and messages Fit with your organization
  • Claude does not know your team's capacity, politics or hidden constraints unless you tell it. Provide them, then review the plan.
  • Ask for options with trade-offs, not only one plan.
  • Treat the output as a first draft that you refine with the team.

5Process Optimization

Step How Claude helps Cedarbrook example
1. Map Turn a description or SOP into a step list or flow Returns: receive, inspect, decide, refund, restock
2. Find bottlenecks Spot waits, rework, hand-offs, manual copying Refund decisions wait for a manager's email
3. Redesign Propose changes: templates, checklists, automation of drafting, clearer rules A decision checklist plus reply templates
4. Pilot Draft a test plan and success measures One warehouse for two weeks
5. Measure Help analyze before/after data and write up results Days to refund, error rate, customer satisfaction
  • Optimize a measurable process: choose KPIs before you start (time, cost, error rate, satisfaction).
  • Claude can augment a step (draft the reply) or redesign the flow (remove an approval) (Module 10).
  • Try changes small first (a pilot), keep humans in review, and expand only on evidence.
Exam tip

Requirements are confirmed by stakeholders, not by Claude: the output is a draft with its assumptions listed for people to check.

Exam tip

Start with use cases where value is high and risk is low, and keep a person in review wherever errors matter.

6Exam Q&A

S1A manager says "Returns take too long." What is the best first use of Claude?

  • AAsk it to redesign the whole customer-care department and write the announcement of the new structure
  • BAsk it to write a press release
  • CAsk it to decide the new policy
  • DAsk it to turn the complaint into clear requirements, assumptions and questions for stakeholders
Show the answer

Answer: D. Clarifying and structuring the need comes first; people then validate it.

S2Which task is the strongest candidate for Claude?

  • AProducing a legally binding contract for a supplier and sending it out with no review at all
  • BDrafting and categorizing hundreds of routine replies that agents review before sending
  • CControlling a warehouse robot in real time
  • DMaking final credit decisions about customers
Show the answer

Answer: B. Text-heavy, repetitive work with human review is a strong fit.

S3A team wants to start using Claude. Which first use case is wisest?

  • ALow-risk and high-value, such as summarizing meeting notes
  • BHigh-risk and high-value, such as automating regulated advice
  • CLow-value and high-risk
  • DWhichever is most complicated
Show the answer

Answer: A. Start with quick wins, learn, and expand carefully.

S4Claude proposes a project plan with a four-week timeline. What should the project manager do?

  • ACheck durations and dependencies against real capacity and constraints, then refine with the team
  • BRemove all risks from the plan
  • CAsk Claude to promise the dates
  • DAdopt it as is
Show the answer

Answer: A. Claude lacks your team's real capacity and hidden constraints.

S5For a comprehensive, cited competitor landscape, which approach fits?

  • AA single web search on the topic, followed by a short summary of the first page
  • BMemory
  • CResearch, then verification of key claims in the sources
  • DExtended thinking only, with no web access and no sources at all
Show the answer

Answer: C. Research gathers multi-source, cited findings; verify the claims you rely on.

S6Which TWO belong at the start of a process-improvement effort? Select TWO.

  • AMap the current steps
  • BSkip baseline data
  • CRemove all reviews
  • DRoll out the new process to everyone at once
  • EChoose measures such as time and error rate
Show the answer

Answer: A, E. Map the process and set the measures before changing anything.

S7Why ask Claude to separate your facts from its assumptions when drafting requirements?

  • ATo make the document longer and to give it a more professional and impressive look
  • BSo that you can verify and correct the assumptions with stakeholders
  • CBecause facts are not needed
  • DBecause assumptions are always right and need no checking by anyone at all
Show the answer

Answer: B. Hidden assumptions are a main source of requirement errors.

S8A team wants to test a redesigned returns checklist. What is a sensible next step?

  • AAsk Claude to declare it a success
  • BSwitch the whole company at once
  • CRun a small pilot with defined success measures
  • DWait a year
Show the answer

Answer: C. A small pilot with defined success measures shows whether the change works before the whole company depends on it.

S9Which factor makes a use case a poor fit for unsupervised Claude?

  • AThe work is repetitive
  • BA mistake would be costly and unlikely to be noticed
  • CThe task is text-based
  • DA person reviews every output
Show the answer

Answer: B. High-cost, unnoticed errors need human review or a different approach.

S10Why provide your own constraints (budget, deadlines, policy) when asking for a plan?

  • AThey are always ignored
  • BThey make the plan less accurate
  • CClaude cannot read them
  • DClaude cannot know them unless you state them, and the plan will fit better with them
Show the answer

Answer: D. Claude cannot know your budget, deadlines or policies unless you state them, and a plan that ignores them will not be realistic.

S11An operations lead wants to replace a manual approval step with Claude's decision on refunds of any size. What is the best response?

  • AUse Claude to draft recommendations and keep a person approving larger or unusual refunds
  • BRemove the refund policy
  • CHide the change from staff
  • DDo it immediately, because Claude applies the refund rules more consistently than the staff do
Show the answer

Answer: A. Keep a human accountable where decisions have financial and customer impact.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Requirements Clarify, structure, find gaps, then validate with people
Facts vs assumptions Ask Claude to separate them; correct the assumptions
Use-case screen Value · fit · risk; start with low-risk, high-value
Strong fit Text-heavy, repetitive, reviewed by a person
Weak fit High-stakes alone, disallowed data, real-time systems, unnoticed costly errors
Research Question, scope, sources; verify claims
Planning Claude drafts; you add real capacity and constraints; ask for options
Process cycle Map · find bottlenecks · redesign · pilot · measure
Measures Choose KPIs before the change
